Search theory for search and rescue planning

Source: R/search.R
ltrlrng.Rd

The quantities a search and rescue planner works with (Koopman's search theory, as used in the U.S. Coast Guard and IAMSAR planning methods):

  • ltrlrng() (lateral range): the probability that a sensor passing at distance x detects the object, under the inverse cube, definite range or M-Beta model with sweep width W;

  • swpwdth() (sweep width): the area under a sampled lateral range curve;

  • srchpod() (search POD): the probability of detection from coverage, for random search, a definite-range sweep and an inverse cube parallel sweep;

  • pswppod() (parallel sweep POD): the POD of a parallel sweep at track spacing S, computed for any model, with optional normal navigation error;

  • srchscs() (search success): the probability of success, the cumulative POD of repeated searches and the containment probabilities updated after an unsuccessful search;

  • datumpmap() (datum probability map): the probability that each grid cell contains the object, for a point, line or area datum;

  • optcrcsrch() (optimal circular search): Koopman's optimal effort for a circular normal datum;

  • opteffort() (optimal effort): the allocation of a fixed effort over cells that maximises the probability of success.

Usage

ltrlrng(x, W, model = c("invcube", "definite", "mbeta"), m = 1, navsd = 0)

swpwdth(x, p = NULL)

srchpod(
  coverage = NULL,
  model = c("random", "definite", "invcube", "mbeta"),
  m = 1,
  W = NULL,
  effort = NULL,
  area = NULL
)

pswppod(
  W,
  S,
  model = c("invcube", "definite", "mbeta"),
  m = 1,
  navsd = 0,
  npts = 2001,
  ntrk = 60
)

srchscs(poc, pod)

datumpmap(
  xedg,
  yedg,
  datum = c("point", "line", "area", "corridor", "general"),
  center = c(0, 0),
  sigma = 1,
  end = NULL,
  nodes = 64,
  wts = NULL
)

optcrcsrch(sigma, W, effort)

opteffort(poc, area = NULL, W, effort, tol = 1e-14)

Arguments

x

Numeric vector: lateral ranges (distances from the track), any sign. For swpwdth(), strictly increasing abscissae, or an rmbl_ltrlrng object (then p is taken from it).

W

Positive number: the sweep width, in the distance unit of the grid and the effort (nautical miles, kilometres: one unit throughout). For srchpod(), give it with effort and area in place of coverage; default NULL.

model

For ltrlrng() and pswppod(): "invcube" (the default), "definite" or "mbeta". For srchpod(): "random" (the default), "definite", "invcube" or "mbeta".

m

Number in (0, 1]: the M-Beta detection probability inside its range. Default 1.

navsd

Non-negative number: the standard deviation of the cross-track navigation error, in the units of x. Default 0.

p

Numeric vector in [0, 1]: the lateral range curve at x.

coverage

Non-negative numeric vector of coverages (sweep width times track length over the area searched; 1 means the effort equals the area). Default NULL: then W, effort and area give it, W * effort / area. Give one or the other, not both.

effort

Non-negative number: the total effort, as track length (the distance the searchers travel while searching, in the unit of W). For srchpod(), the track length in each area, one number or one per area (a matrix laid out like the map when area is one); default NULL.

area

Positive numeric vector, one per cell: the cell areas, in the square of the unit of W. May be NULL when poc is an rmbl_datummap (its cells' areas are used). For srchpod(), the areas searched, or a map from datumpmap() whose cell areas are taken; default NULL.

S

Positive number: the track spacing.

npts, ntrk

Whole numbers: the quadrature points across one spacing (at least 3, raised to the next odd number; default 2001) and the tracks on each side (at least 1; default 60).

poc

Numeric vector or matrix in [0, 1], summing to at most 1: the probability that each area contains the object (your own areas' shares, for example from a consensus of the planners' scenarios). For srchscs() and opteffort() also a probability map from datumpmap(): its cells are the areas, in the order of as.vector(map$poc).

pod

Numeric vector in [0, 1], one per area, or a matrix with one row per search and one column per area. When poc is a map, also a matrix laid out like the map (one search, cell by cell), a srchpod() result with one value per cell, or an opteffort() result (its cells' PODs).

xedg, yedg

Strictly increasing numeric vectors: the cell edges of the grid laid over your search area, east-west and north-south, in the distance unit (seq(-5, 5, by = 0.5): half-unit cells over ten units). Cells may differ in size.

datum

"point" (the default), "line", "area", "corridor" or "general".

center

Two numbers, x then y in the grid's coordinates: the datum point (for example the last known position), the start of a line datum or a corner of an area datum. Default c(0, 0).

sigma

Positive number: the standard deviation of the circular normal position error, in the distance unit (a total probable error E is 1.1774 sigma). Default 1.

end

Two numbers: the end of a line datum or the opposite corner of an area datum; NULL for a point datum.

nodes

Whole number from 2 to 1000: Gauss-Legendre nodes along a line datum. Default 64.

wts

For datum = "general": a non-negative matrix of cell weights, one row per y cell and one column per x cell.

tol

Positive number: the bisection tolerance on log lambda.

Value

ltrlrng(): a numeric vector of class rmbl_ltrlrng (the detection probabilities, with the inputs as attributes; as.numeric() drops them). srchpod(): a numeric vector of class rmbl_srchpod. swpwdth() and pswppod(): one number. srchscs(): a list of class rmbl_srchscs with pos (the probability of success), posarea (per area), pocupd (the updated containment probabilities) and cumpod (the cumulative POD per area), and when poc is a map, map: the map after the unsuccessful search, ready for opteffort() and plot(). datumpmap(): a list of class rmbl_datummap with poc, a matrix with one row per y cell and one column per x cell, outside, and the inputs. optcrcsrch(): a list of class rmbl_optcrc with radius, pos and cntrdns (the coverage at the centre). opteffort(): a list of class rmbl_opteffort with effort, coverage and pod per cell (a matrix when poc is one), pos and lambda. Every class has a print() method, and plot() draws the lateral range curve (equiv = TRUE adds the equivalent definite-range rectangle, spacing a second track), the POD by coverage for any of the models (models, m, cmax), the map as an image with contours, a surface banded by height, the surface and its top view side by side (the device's two panels, or the next two of a layout the caller set with par(mfrow = )), or its cells with their percentages (view), and the allocation (see plot-methods). srchfig draws every figure of Frost (1996) with them.

Details

Coverage is C = W z / A: sweep width times track length over the area searched (for a parallel sweep, W / S). The lateral range curves are: definite range, p(x) = 1 for |x| <= W / 2; M-Beta, p(x) = m for |x| <= W / (2 m); inverse cube, p(x) = 1 - exp(-W^2 / (4 pi x^2)). Each has area W, the sweep width. swpwdth() integrates by the trapezoid rule.

With navsd > 0, ltrlrng() gives the expected curve seen through a normal cross-track navigation error: the convolution of the curve with that normal (Frost 1996, equation 5-14), exact for the rectangular curves and by the trapezoid rule for the inverse cube. Its area is still W; the curve is lower and wider.

srchpod(): random search 1 - exp(-C); definite range min(C, 1); inverse cube parallel sweep erf(sqrt(pi) C / 2) (Koopman 1956); M-Beta parallel sweep C for C < M and 1 - (1 - M)^(C / M) above it (Frost 1996, equation 5-11), which is exact wherever the tracks overlap a whole number of times.

pswppod() integrates over one track spacing (Simpson's rule on npts points) the probability that at least one of the tracks -ntrk, ..., ntrk detects the object; for the inverse cube model the tracks beyond ntrk are added in closed form from sum_k 1 / (x - k S)^2 = (pi / S)^2 / sin^2(pi x / S). With navsd > 0 the lateral range curve is averaged over a normal cross-track error (40-point Gauss-Hermite quadrature). Without navigation error the inverse cube result equals srchpod(W / S, "invcube").

srchscs(): the probability of success is POS = sum(POC * POD); after an unsuccessful search the containment probabilities become POC (1 - POD) / (1 - POS) (Bayes). With several searches (pod a matrix, one row per search) the update is applied in turn and the cumulative POD is 1 - prod(1 - POD) per area. When a search is certain to succeed (POS = 1) the update is undefined: it is returned as NA, with a warning.

datumpmap(): a point datum is a circular normal of standard deviation sigma about center; a line datum the same spread along the segment from center to end (Gauss-Legendre quadrature on nodes points); an area datum a uniform distribution over the rectangle with corners center and end; a corridor datum normal across the segment from center to end and uniform along it, with nothing beyond its ends (Frost 1996, figure 3-8; the segment must run along x or along y); a general datum the cell weights wts scaled to sum to 1. The share of the probability outside the grid is returned as outside.

optcrcsrch(): with effort (track length) L, the optimal search of a circular normal datum covers a disc of radius R = (4 sigma^2 W L / pi)^(1/4), and succeeds with probability 1 - (1 + u) exp(-u), u = R^2 / (2 sigma^2) (Koopman 1957).

opteffort(): under random search detection the optimal effort in cell i is z_i = (A_i / W) log(r_i / lambda) where r_i = POC_i W / A_i exceeds lambda, and 0 elsewhere; the Lagrange multiplier lambda is found by bisection on its logarithm so that the efforts add up to effort (Stone 1975, chapter 2). It assumes random search detection in every cell (the exponential POD curve, srchpod(model = "random")), the conservative choice when the tracks are not laid evenly; a plan searched by parallel sweeps does at least as well.

All distances (x, W, S, navsd, the grid edges, center, end, sigma, effort) are in one unit of your choice, and areas in its square.

Every input is checked: numbers must be finite and of the right length, sweep widths, spacings and standard deviations positive, probabilities in [0, 1] and containment probabilities summing to at most 1; unknown models and datum types are errors.

References

Koopman, B. O. (1946). Search and Screening. OEG Report 56, Operations Evaluation Group, Office of the Chief of Naval Operations.

Koopman, B. O. (1956). The theory of search. I. Kinematic bases. Operations Research 4(3), 324-346. doi:10.1287/opre.4.3.324

Koopman, B. O. (1956). The theory of search. II. Target detection. Operations Research 4(5), 503-531. doi:10.1287/opre.4.5.503

Koopman, B. O. (1957). The theory of search. III. The optimum distribution of searching effort. Operations Research 5(5), 613-626. doi:10.1287/opre.5.5.613

Frost, J. R. (1996). The Theory of Search: A Simplified Explanation. Soza and Company and U.S. Coast Guard Office of Search and Rescue.

Stone, L. D. (1975). Theory of Optimal Search. Academic Press.

Examples

# inverse cube detection 0.5, 1 and 2 sweep widths off the track
ltrlrng(c(0.5, 1, 2), W = 1)
#> ╭── Lateral range curve ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
#> │   Model          inverse cube                                              │
#> │   Sweep width W  1                                                         │
#> │   Ranges         3, from 0.5 to 2                                          │
#> │   Highest pod    0.2726                                                    │
#> │                                                                            │
#> │     range       pod                                                        │
#> │   -------  --------                                                        │
#> │   0.50000  0.272623                                                        │
#> │   1.00000  0.076494                                                        │
#> │   2.00000  0.019698                                                        │
#> │                                                                            │
#> │   inverse cube model, sweep width W = 1                                    │
#> │   pod: the chance of detecting the object at that distance from the track. │
#> │                                                                            │
#> │   The sweep width W is the area under this curve.                          │
#> ╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
plot(ltrlrng(seq(-3, 3, by = 0.5), W = 2))


# the area under the curve is the sweep width
xs <- seq(-200, 200, by = 0.01)
swpwdth(xs, ltrlrng(xs, W = 1, model = "definite"))
#> [1] 1.01

# POD at coverage 1 under the three models
srchpod(1)
#> ╭── Probability of detection ─────────────────────────────────────────╮
#> │   Model      random search                                          │
#> │   Coverages  1                                                      │
#> │                                                                     │
#> │   coverage       pod                                                │
#> │   --------  --------                                                │
#> │          1  0.632121                                                │
#> │                                                                     │
#> │   random search model                                               │
#> │   Coverage is effort over area (sweep width x track length / area); │
#> │   pod is the chance a search at that coverage finds the object.     │
#> ╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
srchpod(c(0.5, 1, 2), model = "invcube")
#> ╭── Probability of detection ─────────────────────────────────────────╮
#> │   Model      inverse cube                                           │
#> │   Coverages  3                                                      │
#> │                                                                     │
#> │   coverage       pod                                                │
#> │   --------  --------                                                │
#> │    0.50000  0.469116                                                │
#> │    1.00000  0.789909                                                │
#> │    2.00000  0.987811                                                │
#> │                                                                     │
#> │   inverse cube model                                                │
#> │   Coverage is effort over area (sweep width x track length / area); │
#> │   pod is the chance a search at that coverage finds the object.     │
#> ╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
plot(srchpod(c(0.5, 1, 1.5)))

# the book's M-Beta curves against random search and the definite range
plot(
  srchpod(1, "mbeta", m = 0.5),
  models = c("random", "definite", "mbeta"),
  m = c(0.5, 0.25)
)

# the expected curve under a navigation error as large as half the sweep
# width
plot(ltrlrng(0, W = 1, navsd = 0.5), equiv = TRUE)


# a parallel sweep at spacing 1.3 W, without and with navigation error
pswppod(1, 1.3)
#> [1] 0.6649981
pswppod(1, 1.3, navsd = 0.3, npts = 201)
#> [1] 0.6460403

# three areas searched once; the containment after finding nothing
srchscs(c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2), c(0.8, 0.5, 0))
#> ╭── Probability of success ────────────────────────────────────────────╮
#> │   Areas        3                                                     │
#> │   Searches     1                                                     │
#> │   Overall POS  0.55                                                  │
#> │                                                                      │
#> │   area     poc  cumpod  posarea  pocupd                              │
#> │   ----  ------  ------  -------  ------                              │
#> │      1  0.5000  0.8000   0.4000  0.2222                              │
#> │      2  0.3000  0.5000   0.1500  0.3333                              │
#> │      3  0.2000  0.0000   0.0000  0.4444                              │
#> │                                                                      │
#> │   POS 0.55 after 1 search                                            │
#> │   poc: chance the object is in the area; cumpod: chance the searches │
#> │   detect it there; pocupd: the poc after the searches found nothing. │
#> ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

# a point datum on a 10 x 10 grid, and the best use of 30 units of track
m <- datumpmap(seq(-5, 5), seq(-5, 5), sigma = 2)
plot(m)

plot(m, view = "both")

# the book's line datum: normal across the line, uniform along it
plot(
  datumpmap(0:10, seq(-3, 3, by = 1.2), "corridor", c(0, 0), end = c(10, 0)),
  view = "cells",
  digits = 1
)

a <- opteffort(m, W = 1, effort = 30)
a$pos
#> [1] 0.4520985
plot(a)

optcrcsrch(sigma = 2, W = 1, effort = 30)$pos
#> [1] 0.4571532

# your own search, step by step: a last known position 2 km east and 3 km
# north of the base, known to about 1.5 km, on a grid of 1 km cells
own <- datumpmap(seq(-3, 7), seq(-2, 8), center = c(2, 3), sigma = 1.5)
own
#> ╭── Datum probability map (point datum) ──────────────────────────────────╮
#> │   Datum   point                                                         │
#> │   Centre  2, 3                                                          │
#> │   Sigma   1.5                                                           │
#> │   Grid    10 x 10 cells (x by y)                                        │
#> │                                                                         │
#> │   The most likely cells                                                 │
#> │       x      y      poc                                                 │
#> │   -----  -----  -------                                                 │
#> │   1.500  2.500  0.06126                                                 │
#> │   1.500  3.500  0.06126                                                 │
#> │   2.500  2.500  0.06126                                                 │
#> │   2.500  3.500  0.06126                                                 │
#> │   0.500  2.500  0.03992                                                 │
#> │                                                                         │
#> │   10 x 10 cells (x by y); 0.2% of the probability lies outside the grid │
#> ╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
# 0.6 km sweep width; 12 km of track walked in each of the four cells round
# the position, none elsewhere
walked <- matrix(0, nrow(own$poc), ncol(own$poc))
walked[5:6, 5:6] <- 12
pd <- srchpod(W = 0.6, effort = walked, area = own, model = "invcube")
# the chance that search found the hiker, and the map if it did not
day1 <- srchscs(own, pd)
day1

day2 <- opteffort(day1$map, W = 0.6, effort = 40)
day2

# inputs that cannot be right are refused
try(ltrlrng(1, W = -1))
#> Error : ltrlrng: `W` must be positive
try(srchpod(1, W = 0.6))
#> Error : srchpod: give either `coverage` or `W`, `effort` and `area`, not both
try(srchscs(c(0.8, 0.8), c(0.5, 0.5)))
#> Error : srchscs: `poc` must sum to at most 1, got 1.6
